Novice Guo Zuo's Affinity for Leaving Home

When I was abbot of Three Conditions Monastery at Pingfang station, about 30 miles south of Harbin, one day in meditation I knew that the next day a young boy would come seeking to leave home. The next morning I told my disciple Guo Neng: "Today a young boy is coming to leave home—when he arrives, let me know."

That noon, Guo Neng came to my room reporting in a Shandong accent: "Master! That young boy you spoke of—he has indeed come!" Going out front, I saw a small boy of twelve or thirteen, handsome and sturdy—plainly the makings of a Bhikshu. Seeing me, he felt as if meeting kin long parted—unable to contain himself, he wept for utter joy.

I asked: "Why do you wish to leave home?" The boy replied: "Because I am ill (at five he could cure others' illnesses, but not his own). Doctors examined me but found no cause, and knew no medicine to cure it. My parents worried greatly, seeking doctors and medicines everywhere, to no avail. One night, in three dreams I saw the same dream-scene. I saw a monk, fat, telling me my illness held no hope of cure—unless I went to Three Conditions Monastery in Harbin, found Dharma Master Anci, and left home under him to cultivate—then the illness would end without medicine. Remembering this clearly, I told my parents and asked leave, then came here to beg Dharma Master Anci in compassion to accept me as disciple."

I smiled and asked on:

Do you know Dharma Master Anci?

I do not know him.

Not knowing him, how will you find him? There is no one here called Dharma Master Anci.

The boy said with utter faith:

There is! The moment I entered the monastery gate, I recognized the fat monk from my dream—and now he sits right here (he pointed at the statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva). He did not lie to me. He told me to come here—no mistake!

I asked on:

What proof is there for anyone to believe your dream? Or is it that you lack clothes, lack food, lack shelter—and so wish to leave home?

The boy insisted:

Not so! I follow exactly this fat Master's guidance (he pointed at Maitreya's statue), telling me to find Dharma Master Anci—for only he can cure my illness. So for over a month I walked more than a thousand miles (then Japan had just surrendered unconditionally, and Manchuria's railways had not yet reopened). Sometimes passing inns, then ahead no villages at all—I had to sleep in open fields. To save time, I only knew to walk on, heedless of all else. One night, sleeping in a field, a pack of wolves suddenly ringed me—but I was not afraid. I told them: "Clear off at once! Refuse, and I'll show no mercy—you'll taste this fruit (a hand grenade)!" Hearing this, the wolves obediently left.

Finishing his tale, the boy looked at me pleadingly. Wishing to test his sincerity, I took a piece of bread, chewed it to mush in my mouth, and spat it on the ground. I told him: "Pick it up and eat it! Eaten, then we'll talk." Without a moment's hesitation or disgust, the boy picked up the saliva-soaked mush and swallowed it down. Such a test sufficed to prove his sincerity and good will toward leaving home—so I consented to his receiving the novice precepts.

After receiving the novice precepts, he applied effort in cultivation, studying eagerly—never lazy, never lax—and within half a year realized the Five Eyes and Six Spiritual Powers, his powers most high—vast spiritual powers indeed. This is no exaggeration—utter fact. Everyone there knew that little novice had spiritual powers. Pity that later he grew proud (arrogant and conceited), inwardly smug, fancying himself most fine—and his powers took wing without a trace; try as he might, he could display them no more.

We cultivators must heed this point. Having spiritual powers is fine, and lacking them is fine too—never grow proud, never cling, still less use them to advertise yourselves. Chiefly, be content with yourselves, vigorous and truly cultivating—toiling with all your might is true skill. With shallow skill yet clinging—to these sounds, those states—deeming them tremendous! Never fall into this—for that is a hundred and eight thousand miles from the Way!

Talks at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall,

Chan Session, July 16 to 23, 1981.
